rv.q: The rich performances make this an unsettling portrait of claustrophobic domesticity and its capacity to warp the mind and the soul.
This inspired production of Pinter’s 1960 blackly comic tale of three misfit men, all dreamers, trying to figure out a way to live.
It may not be the whole truth about Pinter but, in dispensing with awed reverence, it gives the play a renewed vigour and zest.
Warchus's expansive production and the cuddly grotesque at its heart never unnerve you as they should.
Well enough, I’d say, but while he looks the part with wild grey hair, heavy black overcoat and old pinstripe trousers, he’s hobbled rather than helped by aspects of his interpretation.
This is comic strip Pinter. It's a lovingly drawn comic strip, performed with great technical skill and conviction, but it's still a comic strip.
Around me, I have to say, there were adoring playgoers who roared like crazy at the end. I wasn't convinced.
Directed by Matthew Warchus , this is an exceptionally funny rendition of Pinter's blackly comic play.
But there is a cost to being so unambiguously funny... the stakes just feel lower.
While undoubtedly funny, I missed the tension that tightens the nuts and bolts of the play.

cn.t: Spall's cartoonish, highly entertaining performance dominates this comedy-forward revival, though critics are divided on whether the broad, flamboyant approach serves Pinter's 1960 classic well.
